question: According to media reports123, Stephan Kramer, President of the Office for the Protection of the Constitution (AfV) in Thuringia, repeatedly acted in an inadmissible manner in the management of his office, a department of the Thuringian Ministry of the Interior.

He is reported to have passed on chats with journalists to the Thuringian Ministry of the Interior, as a result of which he is facing disciplinary proceedings. In those proceedings, he is accused of ‘serious misconduct’, breach of the ‘general duty of professional secrecy under civil service law’ and of constituting a ‘serious security risk’.

It is also reported that, in dealing with the AfD, he circumvented the unit responsible on several occasions and deliberately failed to consider the question of the immunity of the AfD Members of Parliament concerned in order ‘not to provide arguments to the opponent’.
On several occasions, courts in Thuringia have had to declare measures taken by the Office for the Protection of the Constitution in Thuringia unlawful. 1.
What is the Commission’s assessment of the above in the light of the principles of the rule of law and democracy?

What is the Commission’s view of the failure of the Office for the Protection of the Constitution in Thuringia to take into account the immunity of Thuringian Members of Parliament in the light of EU law?
In this context, what is the Commission's assessment regarding the upholding of the right to good administration (Article 41 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights)?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (8.4.2025) The Commission is fully committed to upholding democracy, the rule of law and fundamental rights in the Member States and will continue to monitor developments at national level.

Concerning the question of the handling of parliamentary immunities by the Office for the Protection of the Constitution in Thuringia, based on the available information, it does not appear that this matter is linked to the implementation of EU law.

The fundamental right to good administration, enshrined in Article 41 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the EU1, aims to fulfil the EU’s commitment to the rule of law, which pursuant to Article 2 of the Treaty on the European Union is one of the EU’s founding values. The right to good administration has also been recognised as a general principle of EU law by the Court of Justice of the EU.

Nevertheless, Article 41 of the Charter is only addressed to the EU’s institutions, bodies, offices and agencies, and not to Member States. For this reason, the Commission is not in a position to assess its application in the context mentioned by the Honourable Member.
1 Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union, OJ C 326, 26.10.2012, p. 391–407.
